summary: This standards-track document defines a YANG data model for managing IP on a device, including configuration and state. It follows the Network Management Datastore Architecture described in RFC 8342. It obsoletes RFC 7277.

plainLanguage.summary: This document defines the standard shape of the IP part of a device's configuration. It says that every network interface has two groups of settings, one for IPv4 and one for IPv6, each holding the addresses on that interface, the mappings from IP addresses to hardware addresses, and a few switches such as whether forwarding is on. A management program can therefore read and write IP settings on any device that follows the model, whatever the vendor.

subtitle: A YANG model for configuring and inspecting IP addresses, neighbours and per-interface settings.

tldr.problem: Network devices are configured and inspected through management protocols, and the IP settings of a device had no agreed shape, so every vendor invented its own.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a YANG module named ietf-ip that adds IPv4 and IPv6 containers to every interface, holding the address list, the neighbour list and the per-interface IP parameters.
tldr.outcome: This version of the model follows the Network Management Datastore Architecture, so the same nodes cover both the configuration a manager intended and the state the device is actually running. It obsoletes RFC 7277.

today: RFC 8344 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the current YANG model for IP management. It replaced RFC 7277, whose earlier version of the model did not follow the Network Management Datastore Architecture.

sections.title: What This Document Defines
sections.content:
The document defines a YANG data model for management of IP implementations. The data model covers configuration of per-interface IPv4 and IPv6 parameters as well as mappings of IP addresses to link-layer addresses. It also provides information about which IP addresses are operationally used and which link-layer mappings exist.

Per-interface parameters are added through augmentation of the interface data model defined in RFC 8343. This version of the IP data model supports the Network Management Datastore Architecture defined in RFC 8342.

The terms client, server, configuration, system state, intended configuration, running configuration datastore, operational state and operational state datastore are defined in RFC 8342 and are not redefined here. The terms augment, data model and data node are defined in RFC 7950, and the terminology for describing YANG data models is found there too. Tree diagrams used in the document follow the notation defined in RFC 8340.
sections.plainLanguage: YANG is a language for describing configuration data, and this document uses it to describe the IP settings of a device. It attaches those settings to each network interface, using the same interface model that the rest of the standards track uses, so that the parts fit together.

sections.title: What Changed from RFC 7277
sections.content:
The ipv4 and ipv6 subtrees with config false data nodes in the /interfaces-state/interface subtree are deprecated. All config false data nodes are now present in the ipv4 and ipv6 subtrees in the /interfaces/interface subtree.

Servers that do not implement the Network Management Datastore Architecture, or that wish to support clients that do not implement it, MAY implement the deprecated ipv4 and ipv6 subtrees in the /interfaces-state/interface subtree.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier version kept the read-only IP state in a separate place from the configuration. This version puts everything in one place per interface, and marks the old location as deprecated so that old software can keep working for now.

sections.title: The Shape of the IP Data Model
sections.content:
The document defines the YANG module ietf-ip, which augments the interface lists defined in the ietf-interfaces module with IP-specific data nodes. Per interface, the module provides two containers, ipv4 and ipv6, representing the two address families. In each container there is a leaf enabled, which controls whether the address family is enabled on that interface, and a leaf forwarding, which controls whether IP packet forwarding for the address family is enabled on the interface.

In each container there is also a list of addresses and a list of mappings from IP addresses to link-layer addresses. The IPv4 container adds the leaf mtu as a uint16, while the IPv6 container adds mtu as a uint32. The IPv4 address list allows the subnet to be given either as a prefix-length or, when the ipv4-non-contiguous-netmasks feature is supported, as a netmask in dotted-quad form. The IPv6 address list carries a read-only status, and the IPv6 neighbour list carries read-only is-router and state leaves. The IPv6 container also has an autoconf branch with leaves for creating global addresses, creating temporary addresses, and the valid and preferred lifetimes of temporary addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Each interface gets two groups of settings, one for each version of IP. Each group has a switch to turn that version on, a switch to turn forwarding on, a maximum packet size, a list of addresses, and a list of known neighbours with the hardware address of each.

sections.title: Relationship to the IP-MIB
sections.content:
If the device implements the IP-MIB, each entry in the ipv4/address and ipv6/address lists is mapped to one ipAddressEntry, where the ipAddressIfIndex refers to the address entry's interface. The IP-MIB defines objects to control IPv6 Router Advertisement messages, and the corresponding YANG data nodes are defined in RFC 8022. The entries in ipv4/neighbor and ipv6/neighbor are mapped to ipNetToPhysicalTable.

The document then gives a table mapping the individual YANG data nodes to the IP-MIB objects they correspond to. The ipv4 container and ipv4/enabled both map to ipv4InterfaceEnableStatus. The ipv4/address list maps to ipAddressEntry, and ipv4/address/ip maps to ipAddressAddrType and ipAddressAddr. The ipv4/neighbor list maps to ipNetToPhysicalEntry, ipv4/neighbor/ip to ipNetToPhysicalNetAddressType and ipNetToPhysicalNetAddress, ipv4/neighbor/link-layer-address to ipNetToPhysicalPhysAddress, and ipv4/neighbor/origin to ipNetToPhysicalType.

On the IPv6 side, ipv6 and ipv6/enabled map to ipv6InterfaceEnableStatus, ipv6/forwarding to ipv6InterfaceForwarding, ipv6/address to ipAddressEntry, ipv6/address/ip to ipAddressAddrType and ipAddressAddr, ipv4/address/origin to ipAddressOrigin, ipv6/address/status to ipAddressStatus, ipv6/neighbor to ipNetToPhysicalEntry, and the ipv6/neighbor leaves map to ipNetToPhysicalNetAddressType, ipNetToPhysicalNetAddress, ipNetToPhysicalPhysAddress, ipNetToPhysicalType and ipNetToPhysicalState.
sections.plainLanguage: Many devices are managed today with SNMP and a table-based model called the IP-MIB. The document lists, node by node, which old table column each new node replaces, so a management program can be written against either and get the same answer.

sections.title: Addresses, Neighbours and Optional Features
sections.content:
The module carries two optional features. The feature ipv4-non-contiguous-netmasks indicates support for configuring non-contiguous subnet masks, and gates the netmask leaf, which has the type yang:dotted-quad. The feature ipv6-privacy-autoconf indicates support for the privacy extensions for stateless address autoconfiguration described in RFC 4941, and gates the temporary-address leaves under autoconf. The create-temporary-addresses leaf is a boolean with a default of false. The temporary-valid-lifetime leaf is a uint32 in seconds with a default of 604800, and the temporary-preferred-lifetime leaf is a uint32 in seconds with a default of 86400.

The example replies show how the model appears over the wire. In the running configuration, an interface named eth0 of type ianaft:ethernetCsmacd carries an IPv4 address of 192.0.2.1 with a prefix length of 24, and an IPv6 address of 2001:db8::10 with a prefix length of 32 and an IPv6 MTU of 1280.

In the operational state, the same interface reports the IPv4 MTU as 1500 with the origin annotation or:system, an IPv4 neighbour 192.0.2.2 with link-layer address 00:00:5E:00:53:AB learned dynamically, and IPv6 neighbours 2001:db8::1 with the same link-layer address, the is-router leaf present and the state reachable, and 2001:db8::4 with the state incomplete and no link-layer address yet. The origin annotation comes from the module ietf-origin and records where each value came from, for example or:default, or:system, or:intended or or:learned.
sections.plainLanguage: The model also records where each value came from, so a management program can tell an address that a person configured from one that a neighbour discovery process learned. Two of the settings are optional: unusual subnet masks, and the temporary IPv6 addresses that hide a user's address.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The document registers a URI in the IETF XML Registry. Following the format in RFC 3688, the registration is the URI urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-ip, with the registrant contact being the NETMOD Working Group of the IETF, and the XML entry recorded as not applicable because the requested URI is an XML namespace.

The document also registers a YANG module in the YANG Module Names registry. The name is ietf-ip, the namespace is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-ip, the prefix is ip, and the reference is RFC 8344.
sections.plainLanguage: The module is given a permanent name and a namespace, so that a program can tell which definition it is looking at and two different models can never be confused with each other.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The YANG module specified in this document defines a schema for data that is designed to be accessed via network management protocols such as NETCONF or RESTCONF. The lowest NETCONF layer is the secure transport layer, and the mandatory-to-implement secure transport is Secure Shell. The lowest RESTCONF layer is HTTPS, and the mandatory-to-implement secure transport is TLS.

The NETCONF access control model provides the means to restrict access for particular NETCONF or RESTCONF users to a preconfigured subset of all available operations and content.

Many data nodes defined in this module are writable, creatable or deletable, since config true is the default, and they may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments. Write operations to these nodes without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations.

The ipv4/enabled and ipv6/enabled leaves are used to enable or disable IPv4 and IPv6 on a specific interface. By enabling a protocol on an interface, an attacker might create an unsecured path into a node, or through it if routing is also enabled; by disabling a protocol, an attacker might force packets to be routed through some other interface or deny access via that protocol. The ipv4/address and ipv6/address lists specify the configured IP addresses, and modifying them can cause a node to ignore messages destined to it or accept messages it would otherwise ignore. The ipv4/forwarding and ipv6/forwarding leaves allow a client to enable or disable forwarding, which can deny service to users or open a conduit into an area. The ipv6/autoconf leaves control the autoconfiguration of IPv6 addresses and whether temporary addresses are used, so modifying them can affect the privacy of the users of the node. Setting the ipv4/mtu and ipv6/mtu leaves to very small values can be used to slow down interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: Almost everything in this model can be changed by a manager, and changing the wrong thing can open a hole or cut a link. The document therefore insists on an encrypted management channel and on access control, and it lists each setting together with the damage an attacker could do with it.

viz.caption: SOME OF THE LEAVES AND WHAT THEY DO

items.title: ipv4/enabled
items.text: Turns IPv4 on or off for that interface.

items.title: ipv4/mtu
items.text: The IPv4 maximum transmission unit, held as a uint16.

items.title: ipv6/mtu
items.text: The IPv6 maximum transmission unit, held as a uint32.

items.title: ipv6/address/status
items.text: Read-only status of an IPv6 address, such as preferred.

items.title: ipv6/neighbor/state
items.text: Read-only state of a neighbour entry, such as reachable.

items.title: ipv6/autoconf
items.text: Controls automatic address creation and the use of temporary addresses.
